source_document.body:

Ford Won't Sell Your Data, and Yes, You Can Still Make Your Smart Car Dumb Again
19 photos
Photo: Ford
Dumb cars have become smart cars with the arsenal of modern technology they’ve received in the last decade, but going back is now possible. Ford’s new Privacy Promise includes options to let users handle what data leaves their cars, and while drivers are put in control of their data, opting out comes with trade-offs. Major trade-offs, to be more precise, as certain big features will be lost once you prevent your car from talking to Ford .
This new Privacy Promise , whose role is to make it easier for drivers to understand what data is being shared with Ford, how the carmaker uses the data, and more importantly, how they can control what they share.
Ford insists on one particular aspect. The data you share with the company is being used to power certain capabilities, including connected services, so once you block the data sharing, your car is going to lose all these capabilities.
For example, the company says that vehicle diagnostics, driving characteristics, and your location are being used for real-time features like embedded navigation, traffic updates, and Roadside Assistance, and to diagnose vehicle issues.
But at the same time, Ford also touts a personalized experience that’s being built with your data, so the company will “offer products, features, and services that are uniquely tailored to you.”
Photo: Ford Because you’re always in control of this data-sharing process, you can block connected vehicle data from leaving your vehicle. “However, in doing so, some features like BlueCruise, Internet connectivity, and vehicle location data on the app will not be usable,” Ford says.
In other words, you’re going to lose all the new-generation features, turning your brand-new Ford into a dumb car again.
But Ford insists on one important part. “We never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers,” the carmaker says.
Your data is still being shared with others, though. Dealers, who need this data “for purposes such as helping with service, warranties, and supporting joint marketing activities,” are among those who work with Ford on this front. Ford’s partners in various spaces, such as customer support and marketing, will also be provided with your data.
What data Ford collects from your car Ford explains that in order to provide you with the full Connected Services and features experience, it’ll need to access the following data:
Vehicle data: the VIN, software version numbers, fuel and fluid levels, tire pressure, engine temperature, the odometer reading, maintenance, vehicle diagnostics, vehicle performance information Driving data: how the vehicle is operated and used - speed, the use of accelerator, brakes, steering, seatbelts Vehicle location: vehicle’s precise latitude and longitude Audio/visual and digital assistant data: images from forward-facing or rear-facing cameras, voice commands when the voice recognition system is in the “active listen” state
If you don’t want to share your location with Ford, you’ll lose the embedded navigation system, Roadside Assistance, the Ford Security package, and the ability to determine where you parked in the Ford app. You’ll still be able to access Android Auto and CarPlay and access the radio and listen to your media.
Photo: Ford The Connected features include software updates, remote features via the Ford app to lock and unlock your car, view the fuel and battery levels, and start and stop the engine. If you enable these features, you also get automatic alerts related to maintenance and be able to activate a Wi-Fi hotspot for up to 10 devices. Block the sharing of data related to Connected features, and you’re left with Android Auto, CarPlay, and a Bluetooth connection for phone calls and music.
Personalized features powered by your data include scheduled maintenance service notifications and other messages, as well as personalized offers “based on your vehicle usage and preferences.” All of these are gone if you block the sharing of data, so all it’s left is a direct communication channel with Ford about recalls, service, and safety.
Eventually, once the data sharing is enabled, you’ll get dealer- and service-related features, including the ability to find services and schedule an appointment with a nearby dealership. If you block the data sharing, you’ll have to do all of that online or directly with a dealer.
Photo: Ford Adjusting how the data sharing works is easy if you own a new-generation Ford. If your car is at least a 2018 model year, you should be able to access all privacy controls directly from the infotainment screen, so when you have a moment, just check out all these options (considering you’re aware of everything you’d be losing once you disable certain options).
Similar controls are also integrated into Ford’s mobile app. Ford says the new Privacy Promise is also applicable to Lincolns, but it will go live in the coming weeks. The same thing will happen for Ford customers in Mexico and Canada, and the carmaker says an expansion to other regions is already on the table, with more details to be shared shortly.
